title: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
summary:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.
"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.
It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".
It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.
It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened.

title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
summary:
'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 yearstoggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty ImagesThe housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.
Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Expensive mortgages are a big factorThe drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.
In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023.
Sponsor MessageHigher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.

(AP Photo/LM Otero)WASHINGTON -- More Americans applied for unemployment benefits last week, but jobless claims remain at historically low levels, layoffs are rare and most workers enjoy unusual job security.
The Labor Department reported Thursday that jobless claims ticked up to 200,000 last week from a revised 191,000 the week before, coming in higher than the 195,000 economists had forecast.

title: Economists Worry Fed Could Go Overboard With Rate Hikes After Hot CPI
summary:
October inflation data came in hot on Tuesday, with consumer prices rising 0.4% month over month.
The hot reading has prompted some senior Fed officials to strike a decidedly more hawkish tone this week.
Austan Goolsbee, the president of the Chicago Fed but not an FOMC voting member, called October's inflation print "borderline disturbing" in an interview with PBS Newshour on Tuesday.
Here's what a few Wall Street economists are saying about the October print and its implications for future Fed policy.
